### I. The Gravity of the Drum

At three hundred miles off the southwest shoulder of Ireland, where the continental shelf abruptly gives up its domestic shelfhood and falls toward the Porcupine Abyssal Plain, the world consists almost entirely of gray heave and hydraulic oil. 

The ship is called the *Aethelgard*, though out here names have very little purchase against the water. She is one hundred and thirty meters of high-tensile steel painted the dull orange of safety cones left out in the sun. Her stern is not rounded like a freighter’s nor squared like a tug’s; it is split by a monumental sheave—a grooved wheel five meters across, rusted at the spokes and polished to a silver mirror along the channel where steel cables have bitten it smooth through forty years of salvage.

Below the main deck, deep in the belly where the ballast tanks groan against the hull, sits the main cable drum. It is twelve meters in diameter, winding slowly under the torque of four planetary gearboxes. When the drum turns, the ship vibrates at a frequency that matches the back of a man’s molars.

Marius stood on the catwalk above the tank, his gloved fingers curled around the rail. Down in the pit, coiled like an endless, sleeping constrictor in layers of chalk and French talc, lay four hundred nautical miles of double-armored submarine fiber-optic cable. 

To the untrained eye, it looked like nothing at all. It was not the majestic, bridge-suspension hawser that tourists imagined when they thought of transoceanic communication. It was barely the thickness of a garden hose. A core of petroleum jelly; six hair-thin tubes of extruded stainless steel; inside those, thirty-six strands of pure silica glass, each no thicker than the lash of an infant’s eye; wrapped in a tube of seamless copper that carried twelve thousand volts of direct current to power the underwater repeaters; wrapped again in high-density polyethylene; and finally, for the sections that would scrape against rock or foul a Spanish trawler’s doors, two opposing layers of galvanized steel wire soaked in bitumen.

Bitumen smells like the edge of a highway being paved in July, combined with the cold, dead iron of an abandoned railway siding. In the hold, where the temperature rarely rose above six degrees Celsius, the smell never faded. It had entered Marius’s skin twenty-five years ago. It was in his coats, his hair, his marriage bed, and the pages of the paperbacks he read during his six-week rotations.

A squawk broke through the heavy thrash of the diesel generators: the bridge intercom, spitting maritime English through a film of salt-crust on the speaker cone.

"Marius. Tension’s coming up on the grapnel. We’re within fifty meters of the charted break."

Marius pressed the talkback button with his forearm. "Understood. Tell the bridge to hold her into the swell. If we broach while the grapnel is hooked into the seabed, we’ll snap the bridle."

"Bridge acknowledges. Sea state five, Marius. Wind’s freshening from the west-southwest. Watch your footing on the gantry."

He didn’t reply. He never replied to reminders about his footing. When a man has spent half his adult life hanging over the stern of a cable ship in a gale, his feet know more about friction and water than his brain ever will.

***

### II. Anatomy of the Cut

Civilization, Marius often thought, did not live in the air. People spoke of the cloud, of the ether, of waves and satellites and invisible light bouncing among orbital constellations. It was a clean, angelic fantasy. It allowed people in bright, air-conditioned rooms in Frankfurt or Singapore to imagine that their thoughts, their speculative bids on grain futures, their private confessions, and their streaming pornography were liberated from the mud.

It was a lie. The cloud was bolted to the earth. More specifically, it was drowned.

Ninety-nine percent of all transoceanic digital traffic did not travel through the sky; it was dragged along the abyssal plains, through trenches deep enough to swallow Everest, over volcanic ridges where superheated hydrothermal fluids hissed through chimneys of iron sulfide. It lay in the dark, subject to the immense, bone-crushing weight of four kilometers of vertical water—four hundred atmospheres of pressure, cold enough that the salt water remained liquid only through its brine, thick as grease.

Down there, nothing happened for ten thousand years. A dusting of diatom shells—marine snow—drifted down through the water column at a rate of one millimeter a century. The carcasses of siphonophores, the moltings of copepods, the microscopic skeletons of radiolarians. And across this infinite, silent terrace of gray-green sediment lay the thread.

Until something went wrong.

The break they were hunting had occurred three days ago at 04:14 UTC. In an instant, thirty-two terabits per second had simply ceased to be. In the control room in Bude, on the Cornish coast, and in the matching station at Halifax, the optical time-domain reflectometers had fired their diagnostic pulses of laser light into the broken fiber. The light traveled down the glass until it reached the ragged end, where it scattered into the salt water. By measuring the precise picosecond return of the backscatter, the machines had done their arithmetic: *Break located at 2,412.87 kilometers from the Halifax terminal. Depth: 3,840 meters.*

The causes were usually mundane. On the shelf, it was almost always an otter board from a bottom-trawler dragging for cod, or a drag-anchor dropped in an emergency by a Chinese box-ship whose chief engineer had lost an engine. But out here, off the shelf, in the deep water? 

Out here, the culprits were stranger. 

Sometimes it was a turbidity current—an underwater avalanche triggered by a tremor so slight no human on land felt it, a roaring river of mud and gravel screaming down the continental slope at sixty miles an hour, snapping four-inch steel like dry spaghetti. 

Sometimes it was an intra-plate fault slip, where two slabs of the planet’s crust ground past each other by half an inch and sheared the cable between them. 

And sometimes, though rarely now that the double-armoring was standard, it was the bite of a hexanchid shark, drawn by the faint electromagnetic hum of the copper power conductor, mistaking the continent-spanning conduit of human chatter for the nervous system of an injured whale, leaving three serrated teeth embedded in the punctured polyethylene.

***

### III. The Hook

On the open working deck, the wind was an iron bar pressed against the chest. The North Atlantic was running long, oily rollers that crested into froth before slamming against the *Aethelgard’s* counter.

The grapple was over the side. It was not a fisherman’s anchor, but a five-ton beast of cast manganese steel called a Gifford grapnel—four curved prongs shaped like the claws of an owl, balanced so that no matter how it tumbled through three miles of black water, at least two hooks would dig into the sea bottom like a plow.

It had taken four hours just to lower it. Four miles of three-inch wire rope, paying out slowly from the winch drum, its weight so monstrous that the brake pads smoked despite the seawater hoses spraying them continuously.

Marius stood beside the tension gauge in the cable shack. The needle was vibrating like an insect’s wing.

"She’s dragging," said MacNair, the winchman. He was an Orkney man with skin that looked like it had been cured in brine and smoked over peat. He never took his eyes off the dial. "Seven tons... seven point five... eight..."

The ship was drifting broadside, her dynamic-positioning thrusters churning the water along her flanks into white cauldrons. The bow thrusters groaned, fighting the wind, holding the vessel to a course perpendicular to the cable path. They were trawling for a wire three miles below their boots, in a place darker than the moon, with no eyes but the strain of a steel wire.

"There," Marius murmured.

The needle didn't jump; it surged. It climbed steadily, smoothly, with a terrifying momentum: *nine tons, twelve tons, sixteen tons.*

"We have it," MacNair said, his thumb already hovering over the hydraulic lever. "Or we’ve hooked Ireland."

"It’s not Ireland," Marius said. "Ireland isn't that elastic."

The tension rose to twenty-two tons. That was the give of the cable: miles of steel armor stretching under the lift, peeling itself out of forty years of silt. 

"Start the haul," Marius ordered. "Slow. Ten meters a minute until we break it clear of the suction."

The winch groaned—a low, mechanical howl that silenced the wind. The hydraulic motors, fed by two thousand pounds of pressure, began their long, rhythmic turn. *Ch-ch-ch-thump. Ch-ch-ch-thump.*

It would take six hours to bring the hook back to the sun.

Marius stepped out onto the windward deck. The salt spray caught him full in the mouth, cold and ancient. He looked down into the water where the wire entered the foam. It went straight down, true as a plumb line, vanishing within ten feet into the bottle-green murk, then into the blue-black, then into the complete, lightless pressure of the abyss.

Down there, the grapnel had bitten into the cable. If the break was clean, the hook would bring up two severed ends, or perhaps only one, hanging limp like the severed tentacle of an octopus. If the cable had wrapped itself around a boulder or caught in a crevice, the tension would spike to fifty tons and the wire rope would part with a sound like a field gun, whipping across the deck to cut a man in two before he heard the report.

They had lost a man that way in '98, on the old *Monarch*, south of the Azores. A Portuguese boy named Joao. Marius had been twenty feet away. He remembered the sound not as an explosion, but as a dull *slap*, like wet butcher’s meat dropped on concrete, and then the boy was simply gone from the waist up, and the winches had kept turning, blind and heavy, winding in the slack wire from the empty sea.

***

### IV. The Microscopic Cathedral

By three in the afternoon, the sky had turned the color of wet zinc. The grapnel broke the surface in a cascade of foam and brown seabed sediment that smelled of rotten eggs and prehistoric cold.

The cable was there.

It hung across two prongs of the Gifford hook, twisted and dripping with gray ooze that sloughed off in thick sheets as the wind caught it. One end trailed down into the sea, still connected to Europe; the other end was a ragged broom of steel wire, frayed and splayed like a brush.

"Hook the stopper lines!" Marius shouted into his chest mic.

The deck crew moved with the methodical, heavy grace of deep-sea workers. There was no running. Running on a wet deck with forty tons of suspended tension is a form of suicide. They threw the chain stoppers around the cable on either side of the hook, shackled them to the deck padeyes, and transferred the load from the winch to the ship’s hull.

Only then did Marius approach the severed end.

He crouched beside it in his yellow oilskins. The gray mud was freezing to the touch; it felt like wet cornstarch, fine as talcum, composed of billions of micro-fossils that had never known the warmth of a sun. He wiped it away with a gloved thumb.

The break was not from an anchor.

The heavy steel wires of the outer armor were pinched, crushed flat, and then pulled until they had thinned to chisel points before parting. The copper tube inside was flattened like a stepped-on drinking straw.

"Submarine slide," MacNair said, leaning over his shoulder, his breath smelling of chicory coffee. "Look at the scour on that polyethylene. It was dragged across basalt."

"Aye," Marius said. "A bank gave way on the slope. Caught it and stretched it until it popped."

"Halifax or Bude?"

"Halifax side," Marius said, pointing to the empty sea. "This is the eastern bight. The western end has probably been carried two miles down the canyon. We’ll have to buoy this end, go fish for the other, splice in three miles of spare from the hold, and bring them together."

"Forty-eight hours on station," MacNair grunted. "The glass men better get their irons hot."

The glass men. That was what the deck hands called the technicians who lived in the cleanroom midships. They were different creatures entirely: men and women who didn't smell of diesel or fish, who wore white anti-static smocks, hairnets, and rubber finger-cots, and who operated in an environment where a single speck of dust or a microscopic tremor could ruin twenty-four hours of work.

An hour later, the severed end was clamped into the traveling gantry and rolled through the airlock into the jointing room.

Here, the ship became a hospital. The walls were white-enameled steel; the air was filtered to five microns; the tables were granite slabs mounted on pneumatic dampers to eliminate the vibration of the ship’s engines.

Marius shed his oilskins in the decontamination vestibule, washed his face in hot water until his skin stopped stinging from the salt, and stepped in his socks into the light.

Elena was already there. She was thirty, half Marius's age, with the long, pale fingers of a concert harpist and the posture of someone who spent eight hours a day looking into an optical microscope.

"How does it look, Marius?"

"Messy. The mud took the armor down to the inner jacket for fifty feet. We’ll have to cut back to the first clean core."

"I’ve got Halifax on the line," she said, nodding toward a monitor displaying a flat green trace. "The terminal station is ready to strike the high voltage the moment we give the all-clear. They’ve rerouted eighty percent of the traffic through the southern loop via Lisbon, but the latency is killing the Frankfurt exchanges. They’re losing four milliseconds per transaction. Some bankers are having apoplexy."

Marius gave a low, dry chuckle. "Four milliseconds. The light has to go an extra six hundred miles around the Azores. Imagine that. The tragedy of it."

"They lose millions, they say."

"They don't lose anything," Marius said, picking up the heavy hydraulic cable shears. "They just don't get it as fast as the other thieves."

He laid the armored cable into the jaws of the cutter. The tool bit down with a muffled *hiss*. Steel wires, one by one, sheared with high-pitched *pings*. Then the copper. Then the inner polyethylene core.

He cut back six feet, then twelve, until the copper tube was round and clean, uncontaminated by salt water. With a surgical scraper, he peeled back the layers until the thirty-six glass cores hung out like clear, flexible horsehair.

They were made of high-purity synthetic fused silica. So pure that if you looked through a block of this glass three miles thick, it would appear as transparent as a clean windowpane.

Elena sat before the fusion splicer. The machine was the size of a breadbox, its interior lit by blue LEDs.

She took one of the fibers—a single strand eighty microns across, coated in a protective lacquer of UV-cured acrylate. With an acetone wipe, she stripped the coating with a single, sharp squeak. Then she placed the bare fiber into a diamond cleaver.

The cleaver was a masterpiece of mechanical precision. A tiny industrial diamond blade scored the glass with a force of less than three grams, then a rubber hammer struck the opposite side, propagating a crack through the silica along its natural crystal plane. The end face of the glass had to be flat to within one-tenth of a single degree. If it had a lip, a hackle, or a slant, the light would bounce off the interior wall and the signal would die in the darkness of the Atlantic.

"Cleave angle zero point one two," Elena muttered, looking at the display. "Good enough for the pope."

She laid the fiber into the V-groove of the splicer. Opposite it, she placed the corresponding fiber from the spare cable coiled in the hold below.

Through the microscope, displayed on a high-resolution screen, the two fiber ends looked like two massive glass pillars, smooth and translucent, suspended in a void. Between them was a gap of five microns.

"Aligning," she said.

Stepping motors moved the glass pillars in increments of nanometers. The machine fired an image-processing algorithm, looking at the way light from an internal LED passed through the cores.

"Core-to-core match. Offset zero point zero three microns."

"Burn it," Marius said.

Elena pressed the red button.

Between two tungsten electrodes, an electric arc flashed—a purple spark, tiny as an ember, lasting two-tenths of a second. The heat was eighteen hundred degrees Celsius. The glass softened, flowed, and became one.

On the screen, the boundary between the two pillars vanished. Where there had been two, there was now only a single, unbroken column of glass.

"Loss," Elena read from the instrument. "Zero point zero one decibels. Perfect."

She did not smile. She had thirty-five more to do on this side, and then the whole process would be repeated for the western bight once they retrieved it from the canyon floor. Thirty-six strands of light. Each strand carrying forty separate wavelengths of infrared laser light. Each wavelength carrying one hundred gigabits of human longing, greed, boredom, and terror every second.

***

### V. The Drift

That night, the wind backed into the north and dropped the temperature below freezing. The salt on the *Aethelgard’s* rigging turned to rime, coating the stays in coats of white fur that rattled like dry bones whenever the ship rolled.

Marius couldn't sleep. It was always like this between the splices. The ship was "hanging on the bight"—the cable was secured to the heavy deck cranes, supporting the weight of three miles of wire that hung between the ship and the seabed like a gigantic catenary curve.

If a storm blew up suddenly, or if an engine failed and the dynamic positioning lost its fix, the ship would drift. The cable would come tight against the stern. It would reach its breaking limit, and then it would part, and thirty-six hours of work would be erased in a second, whistling back into the depths to be buried in the mud forever.

He walked up to the bridge. It was darkened, illuminated only by the faint red glow of the radar screens and the sea-green wash of the electronic navigation charts.

The second mate, a young Finn named Lindqvist, was on watch, leaning against the central console with a mug of tea between his palms.

"How are we holding, Mr. Lindqvist?"

"Ten knots from the north-northwest," the Finn said without turning. "Thrusters are running at thirty percent. She’s sitting like an island, Marius. Don't worry so much. You’ll have an ulcer."

"I have an ulcer," Marius said. "I’ve had one since the seventies."

He looked out through the heated windows. The Atlantic was black, invisible save for the white crests that tore themselves apart against the bow.

He thought about what was moving through that glass down in the hold.

Right now, because the splice was half-finished, the western end was dark. But the eastern end was still alive, talking to itself. Halifax was dark, but Bude was pulsing. The repeaters along the seabed—torpedo-shaped cylinders of beryllium copper spaced every sixty miles along the ocean floor—were still being powered by the high-voltage conductor.

The terminal stations were running "loop-back" diagnostics. They were firing endless strings of pseudo-random numbers into the dark, waiting for them to bounce off the open cut and return to the Cornish coast.

*0101110010100011101...*

It was a language that had no speaker and no listener. It was the background radiation of the human animal.

Marius remembered his grandfather, who had been a telegraphist for the Eastern Telegraph Company in Porthcurno. The old man had sat in a granite room with a brass key and a paper tape, listening to the clicks that represented the fall of Khartoum or the death of Queen Victoria. In those days, a word cost four shillings. People chose their adjectives with the care of diamond cutters. They did not say: *I am sitting at an airport terminal eating an overpriced sandwich and feeling slightly melancholy.* They said: *ARRIVING TUESDAY. LOVE.*

Now, the cable was stuffed with everything. 

Every second, millions of images of faces that would never be remembered, bank transfers that existed only as balance shifts between electronic ledgers, surveillance footage from street corners in Leeds, updates to smartphone applications that changed the shade of an icon from turquoise to seafoam, love letters typed by thumbs in the dark, algorithmic orders to purchase six million bushels of soy before the Chicago bell, hatreds fermented in message boards, apologies that arrived too late, photographs of dinner plates, maps of places nobody was going.

All of it converted into pulses of infrared light at 1,550 nanometers. Photons traveling through silica glass at two hundred thousand kilometers per second—slowed down by thirty percent because even the purest glass is thicker than a vacuum, but still fast enough to circle the planet eight times in the time it takes a man to draw a breath.

And it was all resting on the mud.

Down where the *Bathynomus giganteus*—the giant isopods, pale and blind as scrub-brushes—crawled over the armor wires. Down where the cold water was four hundred times denser than the air. Down where there was no winter, no summer, no morning, no war, no music, only the absolute, thermodynamic stillness of the floor of the world.

The cable didn't care about the messages. The glass did not remember the light that passed through it. Once the photon cleared the fiber and struck the photodiode in the receiver, the glass was dark again, clear and empty, waiting for the next pulse.

***

### VI. The Burial

By noon the following day, the sea had smoothed into a long, heavy swell that looked like hammered pewter.

The second splice was complete. The western bight had been grappled from the canyon mouth, hauled up, cut back, cleaved, fused, and tested.

Now came the delicate part: the casing.

Around the bare fibers, Elena and Marius had clamped a stainless-steel sleeve, injecting it with polyurethane resin that set as hard as granite. Over that, they slipped a copper sleeve, crimping it to the original copper power tube with a five-hundred-ton hydraulic press to ensure the 12,000-volt circuit was continuous. Then the layers of high-tensile steel wire were woven back together by hand—a process called "wire-serving"—each wire tucked into its original groove with a wooden mallet and a marlinspike, until the joint looked like a long, metallic swell, five meters long and heavy as an anvil.

Finally, they wrapped the whole assembly in thick bands of asphalt-impregnated jute, smearing it with hot bitumen until it was black, sticky, and impenetrable.

"Joint 44-Foxtrot ready for the chute," Marius called out.

The deck crew assembled around the bight. The joint was heavy—nearly half a ton. It sat on wooden skids, held by nylon strops.

The *Aethelgard* was positioned directly over the lay-path.

"Pay out slowly," Marius commanded. "Don't let it twist. If the joint rotates while it’s going over the stern sheave, we’ll kink the armor."

The crane lifted the joint into the air. It hung between sea and sky, black and glistening, dripping tar onto the orange deck.

The great five-meter wheel at the stern began to turn. The joint settled into the groove with a heavy *thud*. It rolled slowly over the crown of the wheel, tilting down toward the water.

Marius stood on the stern platform, right over the thruster wash. The spray was warm compared to the air, tasting of salt and sulfur.

"Lower away."

The joint slipped into the water. For a moment, it remained visible—a long, dark shape sliding through the turquoise boil of the propellers—and then it was gone.

The tension gauge climbed: *two tons, five tons, eight tons.*

The cable was sinking. It was falling back down through the water column. It would take forty-five minutes for that joint to hit the bottom. It would drop through the sunlight zone, through the twilight zone where the lanternfish blinked their rows of photophores, through the midnight zone where the water was four degrees, down to the soft, welcoming bed of gray diatomaceous ooze.

It would settle with a faint, imperceptible puff of mud, like a sleeper turning over in a feather bed. The silt would rise up, drift for an hour in the deep, sluggish bottom currents, and then slowly settle back down, covering the black tar and the bright steel with a microscopic blanket of dust.

In a hundred years, it would be buried three inches deep. In ten thousand years, it would be a fossil—a horizontal vein of copper, silica, and iron running through the stratigraphic layer of the Holocene, like the track of a prehistoric worm that had crawled across the seabed and died there.

***

### VII. Light Resumes

In the cleanroom, the red lights were gone.

Elena was packing her diamond cleavers into their velvet-lined mahogany cases. She looked tired; her eyes were red-rimmed, and she had a smear of graphite grease on her chin.

On the main terminal monitor, the flat green trace had vanished. In its place was a chaotic, beautiful dance of numbers: data rates, signal-to-noise ratios, eye diagrams that showed the digital pulses opening up like wide, almond-shaped pupils.

"Bude has closed the circuit," she said quietly. "Halifax has brought the voltage up to eleven thousand. Loop current is one point six amperes."

"And the traffic?" Marius asked.

She clicked a mouse. A diagnostic window opened.

"They’re cut over. The Lisbon loop is relieved. Full bandwidth restored."

Marius looked at the screen. The numbers were too fast to read. Millions of bits becoming billions, becoming trillions. 

Somewhere in a basement in New Jersey, a server had just confirmed the delivery of an encrypted email sent from a basement in Utrecht. Somewhere in an apartment in Paris, a boy was watching a video of a girl singing in a kitchen in Montreal, her voice broken into pieces, turned into light, sent down through the rocks and the cold ooze, and reassembled in his headphones so cleanly he could hear her inhale between the lines.

None of them knew about the *Aethelgard*. None of them knew about the Gifford grapnel dragging its claws through three miles of mud, or the purple arc that had burned for two-tenths of a second between two tungsten needles, or the bitumen under Marius’s fingernails that would take three weeks of lemon juice and pumice to remove.

"They’re happy," Elena said, pointing to a message scrolling on the service channel from the Halifax engineer: *LOSS WITHIN SPEC. GOOD JOB AETHELGARD. DRINK ONE FOR US.*

"Aye," Marius said.

He picked up his oily gloves from the bench and stuffed them into his coat pocket.

"Come on," he said. "The cook’s made potato soup with salt pork. It’ll be cold if we don't get there before the deck apes eat it all."

***

### VIII. The Turn

They walked out onto the working deck together.

The cable was gone. The stern sheave was still, its groove wet and empty, reflecting the gray sky. The crane had been boomed down and lashed into its cradle with turnbuckles. The deck had been hosed down, though the smell of sea-mud and old tar still hung thick in the cold air.

The ship’s horn gave three long, rumbling blasts that shook the water out of the lifeboats.

The *Aethelgard* was turning. Her bow rose as she met the swell head-on, throwing two great wings of spray thirty feet into the air. The engines changed their note from the high-pitched whine of station-keeping to the deep, resonant thrum of transit.

Twelve knots. Heading east-southeast. Toward the mouth of the English Channel, then the Solent, then the dock at Southampton where four hundred more miles of armored cable were waiting on the quay to be loaded into the hold by hand, strand by strand, layer by layer, with chalk and French talc to keep it from sticking.

Marius leaned against the bulwark and pulled a cigarette from his tin. He shielded it with his coat, struck the match, and took the smoke deep into his chest.

Behind them, the Porcupine Abyssal Plain was smooth again. 

Four kilometers below the ship’s white wake, in the cold that had no name and the dark that had never seen an eye, the glass thread lay motionless in the mud. 

Inside it, unseen, unfelt, and silent as prayer, the light was running.

By measuring the precise picosecond return of the backscatter, the machines had done their arithmetic: *Break located at 2,412.87 kilometers from the Halifax terminal. Depth: 3,840 meters.*

The causes were usually mundane. On the shelf, it was almost always an otter board from a bottom-trawler dragging for cod, or a drag-anchor dropped in an emergency by a Chinese box-ship whose chief engineer had lost an engine. But out here, off the shelf, in the deep water? 

Out here, the culprits were stranger. 

Sometimes it was a turbidity current—an underwater avalanche triggered by a tremor so slight no human on land felt it, a roaring river of mud and gravel screaming down the continental slope at sixty miles an hour, snapping four-inch steel like dry spaghetti. 

Sometimes it was an intra-plate fault slip, where two slabs of the planet’s crust ground past each other by half an inch and sheared the cable between them. 

And sometimes, though rarely now that the double-armoring was standard, it was the bite of a hexanchid shark, drawn by the faint electromagnetic hum of the copper power conductor, mistaking the continent-spanning conduit of human chatter for the nervous system of an injured whale, leaving three serrated teeth embedded in the punctured polyethylene.

***

### III. The Hook

On the open working deck, the wind was an iron bar pressed against the chest. The North Atlantic was running long, oily rollers that crested into froth before slamming against the *Aethelgard’s* counter.

The grapple was over the side. It was not a fisherman’s anchor, but a five-ton beast of cast manganese steel called a Gifford grapnel—four curved prongs shaped like the claws of an owl, balanced so that no matter how it tumbled through three miles of black water, at least two hooks would dig into the sea bottom like a plow.

It had taken four hours just to lower it. Four miles of three-inch wire rope, paying out slowly from the winch drum, its weight so monstrous that the brake pads smoked despite the seawater hoses spraying them continuously.

Marius stood beside the tension gauge in the cable shack. The needle was vibrating like an insect’s wing.

"She’s dragging," said MacNair, the winchman. He was an Orkney man with skin that looked like it had been cured in brine and smoked over peat. He never took his eyes off the dial. "Seven tons... seven point five... eight..."

The ship was drifting broadside, her dynamic-positioning thrusters churning the water along her flanks into white cauldrons. The bow thrusters groaned, fighting the wind, holding the vessel to a course perpendicular to the cable path. They were trawling for a wire three miles below their boots, in a place darker than the moon, with no eyes but the strain of a steel wire.

"There," Marius murmured.

The needle didn't jump; it surged. It climbed steadily, smoothly, with a terrifying momentum: *nine tons, twelve tons, sixteen tons.*

"We have it," MacNair said, his thumb already hovering over the hydraulic lever. "Or we’ve hooked Ireland."

"It’s not Ireland," Marius said. "Ireland isn't that elastic."

The tension rose to twenty-two tons. That was the give of the cable: miles of steel armor stretching under the lift, peeling itself out of forty years of silt. 

"Start the haul," Marius ordered. "Slow. Ten meters a minute until we break it clear of the suction."

The winch groaned—a low, mechanical howl that silenced the wind. The hydraulic motors, fed by two thousand pounds of pressure, began their long, rhythmic turn. *Ch-ch-ch-thump. Ch-ch-ch-thump.*

It would take six hours to bring the hook back to the sun.

Marius stepped out onto the windward deck. The salt spray caught him full in the mouth, cold and ancient. He looked down into the water where the wire entered the foam. It went straight down, true as a plumb line, vanishing within ten feet into the bottle-green murk, then into the blue-black, then into the complete, lightless pressure of the abyss.

Down there, the grapnel had bitten into the cable. If the break was clean, the hook would bring up two severed ends, or perhaps only one, hanging limp like the severed tentacle of an octopus. If the cable had wrapped itself around a boulder or caught in a crevice, the tension would spike to fifty tons and the wire rope would part with a sound like a field gun, whipping across the deck to cut a man in two before he heard the report.

They had lost a man that way in '98, on the old *Monarch*, south of the Azores. A Portuguese boy named Joao. Marius had been twenty feet away. He remembered the sound not as an explosion, but as a dull *slap*, like wet butcher’s meat dropped on concrete, and then the boy was simply gone from the waist up, and the winches had kept turning, blind and heavy, winding in the slack wire from the empty sea.

***

### IV. The Microscopic Cathedral

By three in the afternoon, the sky had turned the color of wet zinc. The grapnel broke the surface in a cascade of foam and brown seabed sediment that smelled of rotten eggs and prehistoric cold.

The cable was there.

It hung across two prongs of the Gifford hook, twisted and dripping with gray ooze that sloughed off in thick sheets as the wind caught it. One end trailed down into the sea, still connected to Europe; the other end was a ragged broom of steel wire, frayed and splayed like a brush.

"Hook the stopper lines!" Marius shouted into his chest mic.

The deck crew moved with the methodical, heavy grace of deep-sea workers. There was no running. Running on a wet deck with forty tons of suspended tension is a form of suicide. They threw the chain stoppers around the cable on either side of the hook, shackled them to the deck padeyes, and transferred the load from the winch to the ship’s hull.

Only then did Marius approach the severed end.

He crouched beside it in his yellow oilskins. The gray mud was freezing to the touch; it felt like wet cornstarch, fine as talcum, composed of billions of micro-fossils that had never known the warmth of a sun. He wiped it away with a gloved thumb.

The break was not from an anchor.

The heavy steel wires of the outer armor were pinched, crushed flat, and then pulled until they had thinned to chisel points before parting. The copper tube inside was flattened like a stepped-on drinking straw.

"Submarine slide," MacNair said, leaning over his shoulder, his breath smelling of chicory coffee. "Look at the scour on that polyethylene. It was dragged across basalt."

"Aye," Marius said. "A bank gave way on the slope. Caught it and stretched it until it popped."

"Halifax or Bude?"

"Halifax side," Marius said, pointing to the empty sea. "This is the eastern bight. The western end has probably been carried two miles down the canyon. We’ll have to buoy this end, go fish for the other, splice in three miles of spare from the hold, and bring them together."

"Forty-eight hours on station," MacNair grunted. "The glass men better get their irons hot."

The glass men. That was what the deck hands called the technicians who lived in the cleanroom midships. They were different creatures entirely: men and women who didn't smell of diesel or fish, who wore white anti-static smocks, hairnets, and rubber finger-cots, and who operated in an environment where a single speck of dust or a microscopic tremor could ruin twenty-four hours of work.

An hour later, the severed end was clamped into the traveling gantry and rolled through the airlock into the jointing room.

Here, the ship became a hospital. The walls were white-enameled steel; the air was filtered to five microns; the tables were granite slabs mounted on pneumatic dampers to eliminate the vibration of the ship’s engines.

Marius shed his oilskins in the decontamination vestibule, washed his face in hot water until his skin stopped stinging from the salt, and stepped in his socks into the light.

Elena was already there. She was thirty, half Marius's age, with the long, pale fingers of a concert harpist and the posture of someone who spent eight hours a day looking into an optical microscope.

"How does it look, Marius?"

"Messy. The mud took the armor down to the inner jacket for fifty feet. We’ll have to cut back to the first clean core."

"I’ve got Halifax on the line," she said, nodding toward a monitor displaying a flat green trace. "The terminal station is ready to strike the high voltage the moment we give the all-clear. They’ve rerouted eighty percent of the traffic through the southern loop via Lisbon, but the latency is killing the Frankfurt exchanges. They’re losing four milliseconds per transaction. Some bankers are having apoplexy."

Marius gave a low, dry chuckle. "Four milliseconds. The light has to go an extra six hundred miles around the Azores. Imagine that. The tragedy of it."

"They lose millions, they say."

"They don't lose anything," Marius said, picking up the heavy hydraulic cable shears. "They just don't get it as fast as the other thieves."

He laid the armored cable into the jaws of the cutter. The tool bit down with a muffled *hiss*. Steel wires, one by one, sheared with high-pitched *pings*. Then the copper. Then the inner polyethylene core.

He cut back six feet, then twelve, until the copper tube was round and clean, uncontaminated by salt water. With a surgical scraper, he peeled back the layers until the thirty-six glass cores hung out like clear, flexible horsehair.

They were made of high-purity synthetic fused silica. So pure that if you looked through a block of this glass three miles thick, it would appear as transparent as a clean windowpane.

Elena sat before the fusion splicer. The machine was the size of a breadbox, its interior lit by blue LEDs.

She took one of the fibers—a single strand eighty microns across, coated in a protective lacquer of UV-cured acrylate. With an acetone wipe, she stripped the coating with a single, sharp squeak. Then she placed the bare fiber into a diamond cleaver.

The cleaver was a masterpiece of mechanical precision. A tiny industrial diamond blade scored the glass with a force of less than three grams, then a rubber hammer struck the opposite side, propagating a crack through the silica along its natural crystal plane. The end face of the glass had to be flat to within one-tenth of a single degree. If it had a lip, a hackle, or a slant, the light would bounce off the interior wall and the signal would die in the darkness of the Atlantic.

"Cleave angle zero point one two," Elena muttered, looking at the display. "Good enough for the pope."

She laid the fiber into the V-groove of the splicer. Opposite it, she placed the corresponding fiber from the spare cable coiled in the hold below.

Through the microscope, displayed on a high-resolution screen, the two fiber ends looked like two massive glass pillars, smooth and translucent, suspended in a void. Between them was a gap of five microns.

"Aligning," she said.

Stepping motors moved the glass pillars in increments of nanometers. The machine fired an image-processing algorithm, looking at the way light from an internal LED passed through the cores.

"Core-to-core match. Offset zero point zero three microns."

"Burn it," Marius said.

Elena pressed the red button.

Between two tungsten electrodes, an electric arc flashed—a purple spark, tiny as an ember, lasting two-tenths of a second. The heat was eighteen hundred degrees Celsius. The glass softened, flowed, and became one.

On the screen, the boundary between the two pillars vanished. Where there had been two, there was now only a single, unbroken column of glass.

"Loss," Elena read from the instrument. "Zero point zero one decibels. Perfect."

She did not smile. She had thirty-five more to do on this side, and then the whole process would be repeated for the western bight once they retrieved it from the canyon floor. Thirty-six strands of light. Each strand carrying forty separate wavelengths of infrared laser light. Each wavelength carrying one hundred gigabits of human longing, greed, boredom, and terror every second.

***

### V. The Drift

That night, the wind backed into the north and dropped the temperature below freezing. The salt on the *Aethelgard’s* rigging turned to rime, coating the stays in coats of white fur that rattled like dry bones whenever the ship rolled.

Marius couldn't sleep. It was always like this between the splices. The ship was "hanging on the bight"—the cable was secured to the heavy deck cranes, supporting the weight of three miles of wire that hung between the ship and the seabed like a gigantic catenary curve.

If a storm blew up suddenly, or if an engine failed and the dynamic positioning lost its fix, the ship would drift. The cable would come tight against the stern. It would reach its breaking limit, and then it would part, and thirty-six hours of work would be erased in a second, whistling back into the depths to be buried in the mud forever.

He walked up to the bridge. It was darkened, illuminated only by the faint red glow of the radar screens and the sea-green wash of the electronic navigation charts.

The second mate, a young Finn named Lindqvist, was on watch, leaning against the central console with a mug of tea between his palms.

"How are we holding, Mr. Lindqvist?"

"Ten knots from the north-northwest," the Finn said without turning. "Thrusters are running at thirty percent. She’s sitting like an island, Marius. Don't worry so much. You’ll have an ulcer."

"I have an ulcer," Marius said. "I’ve had one since the seventies."

He looked out through the heated windows. The Atlantic was black, invisible save for the white crests that tore themselves apart against the bow.

He thought about what was moving through that glass down in the hold.

Right now, because the splice was half-finished, the western end was dark. But the eastern end was still alive, talking to itself. Halifax was dark, but Bude was pulsing. The repeaters along the seabed—torpedo-shaped cylinders of beryllium copper spaced every sixty miles along the ocean floor—were still being powered by the high-voltage conductor.

The terminal stations were running "loop-back" diagnostics. They were firing endless strings of pseudo-random numbers into the dark, waiting for them to bounce off the open cut and return to the Cornish coast.

*0101110010100011101...*

It was a language that had no speaker and no listener. It was the background radiation of the human animal.

Marius remembered his grandfather, who had been a telegraphist for the Eastern Telegraph Company in Porthcurno. The old man had sat in a granite room with a brass key and a paper tape, listening to the clicks that represented the fall of Khartoum or the death of Queen Victoria. In those days, a word cost four shillings. People chose their adjectives with the care of diamond cutters. They did not say: *I am sitting at an airport terminal eating an overpriced sandwich and feeling slightly melancholy.* They said: *ARRIVING TUESDAY. LOVE.*

Now, the cable was stuffed with everything. 

Every second, millions of images of faces that would never be remembered, bank transfers that existed only as balance shifts between electronic ledgers, surveillance footage from street corners in Leeds, updates to smartphone applications that changed the shade of an icon from turquoise to seafoam, love letters typed by thumbs in the dark, algorithmic orders to purchase six million bushels of soy before the Chicago bell, hatreds fermented in message boards, apologies that arrived too late, photographs of dinner plates, maps of places nobody was going.

All of it converted into pulses of infrared light at 1,550 nanometers. Photons traveling through silica glass at two hundred thousand kilometers per second—slowed down by thirty percent because even the purest glass is thicker than a vacuum, but still fast enough to circle the planet eight times in the time it takes a man to draw a breath.

And it was all resting on the mud.

Down where the *Bathynomus giganteus*—the giant isopods, pale and blind as scrub-brushes—crawled over the armor wires. Down where the cold water was four hundred times denser than the air. Down where there was no winter, no summer, no morning, no war, no music, only the absolute, thermodynamic stillness of the floor of the world.

The cable didn't care about the messages. The glass did not remember the light that passed through it. Once the photon cleared the fiber and struck the photodiode in the receiver, the glass was dark again, clear and empty, waiting for the next pulse.

***

### VI. The Burial

By noon the following day, the sea had smoothed into a long, heavy swell that looked like hammered pewter.

The second splice was complete. The western bight had been grappled from the canyon mouth, hauled up, cut back, cleaved, fused, and tested.

Now came the delicate part: the casing.

Around the bare fibers, Elena and Marius had clamped a stainless-steel sleeve, injecting it with polyurethane resin that set as hard as granite. Over that, they slipped a copper sleeve, crimping it to the original copper power tube with a five-hundred-ton hydraulic press to ensure the 12,000-volt circuit was continuous. Then the layers of high-tensile steel wire were woven back together by hand—a process called "wire-serving"—each wire tucked into its original groove with a wooden mallet and a marlinspike, until the joint looked like a long, metallic swell, five meters long and heavy as an anvil.

Finally, they wrapped the whole assembly in thick bands of asphalt-impregnated jute, smearing it with hot bitumen until it was black, sticky, and impenetrable.

"Joint 44-Foxtrot ready for the chute," Marius called out.

The deck crew assembled around the bight. The joint was heavy—nearly half a ton. It sat on wooden skids, held by nylon strops.

The *Aethelgard* was positioned directly over the lay-path.

"Pay out slowly," Marius commanded. "Don't let it twist. If the joint rotates while it’s going over the stern sheave, we’ll kink the armor."

The crane lifted the joint into the air. It hung between sea and sky, black and glistening, dripping tar onto the orange deck.

The great five-meter wheel at the stern began to turn. The joint settled into the groove with a heavy *thud*. It rolled slowly over the crown of the wheel, tilting down toward the water.

Marius stood on the stern platform, right over the thruster wash. The spray was warm compared to the air, tasting of salt and sulfur.

"Lower away."

The joint slipped into the water. For a moment, it remained visible—a long, dark shape sliding through the turquoise boil of the propellers—and then it was gone.

The tension gauge climbed: *two tons, five tons, eight tons.*

The cable was sinking. It was falling back down through the water column. It would take forty-five minutes for that joint to hit the bottom. It would drop through the sunlight zone, through the twilight zone where the lanternfish blinked their rows of photophores, through the midnight zone where the water was four degrees, down to the soft, welcoming bed of gray diatomaceous ooze.

It would settle with a faint, imperceptible puff of mud, like a sleeper turning over in a feather bed. The silt would rise up, drift for an hour in the deep, sluggish bottom currents, and then slowly settle back down, covering the black tar and the bright steel with a microscopic blanket of dust.

In a hundred years, it would be buried three inches deep. In ten thousand years, it would be a fossil—a horizontal vein of copper, silica, and iron running through the stratigraphic layer of the Holocene, like the track of a prehistoric worm that had crawled across the seabed and died there.

***

### VII. Light Resumes

In the cleanroom, the red lights were gone.

Elena was packing her diamond cleavers into their velvet-lined mahogany cases. She looked tired; her eyes were red-rimmed, and she had a smear of graphite grease on her chin.

On the main terminal monitor, the flat green trace had vanished. In its place was a chaotic, beautiful dance of numbers: data rates, signal-to-noise ratios, eye diagrams that showed the digital pulses opening up like wide, almond-shaped pupils.

"Bude has closed the circuit," she said quietly. "Halifax has brought the voltage up to eleven thousand. Loop current is one point six amperes."

"And the traffic?" Marius asked.

She clicked a mouse. A diagnostic window opened.

"They’re cut over. The Lisbon loop is relieved. Full bandwidth restored."

Marius looked at the screen. The numbers were too fast to read. Millions of bits becoming billions, becoming trillions. 

Somewhere in a basement in New Jersey, a server had just confirmed the delivery of an encrypted email sent from a basement in Utrecht. Somewhere in an apartment in Paris, a boy was watching a video of a girl singing in a kitchen in Montreal, her voice broken into pieces, turned into light, sent down through the rocks and the cold ooze, and reassembled in his headphones so cleanly he could hear her inhale between the lines.

None of them knew about the *Aethelgard*. None of them knew about the Gifford grapnel dragging its claws through three miles of mud, or the purple arc that had burned for two-tenths of a second between two tungsten needles, or the bitumen under Marius’s fingernails that would take three weeks of lemon juice and pumice to remove.

"They’re happy," Elena said, pointing to a message scrolling on the service channel from the Halifax engineer: *LOSS WITHIN SPEC. GOOD JOB AETHELGARD. DRINK ONE FOR US.*

"Aye," Marius said.

He picked up his oily gloves from the bench and stuffed them into his coat pocket.

"Come on," he said. "The cook’s made potato soup with salt pork. It’ll be cold if we don't get there before the deck apes eat it all."

***

### VIII. The Turn

They walked out onto the working deck together.

The cable was gone. The stern sheave was still, its groove wet and empty, reflecting the gray sky. The crane had been boomed down and lashed into its cradle with turnbuckles. The deck had been hosed down, though the smell of sea-mud and old tar still hung thick in the cold air.

The ship’s horn gave three long, rumbling blasts that shook the water out of the lifeboats.

The *Aethelgard* was turning. Her bow rose as she met the swell head-on, throwing two great wings of spray thirty feet into the air. The engines changed their note from the high-pitched whine of station-keeping to the deep, resonant thrum of transit.

Twelve knots. Heading east-southeast. Toward the mouth of the English Channel, then the Solent, then the dock at Southampton where four hundred more miles of armored cable were waiting on the quay to be loaded into the hold by hand, strand by strand, layer by layer, with chalk and French talc to keep it from sticking.

Marius leaned against the bulwark and pulled a cigarette from his tin. He shielded it with his coat, struck the match, and took the smoke deep into his chest.

Behind them, the Porcupine Abyssal Plain was smooth again. 

Four kilometers below the ship’s white wake, in the cold that had no name and the dark that had never seen an eye, the glass thread lay motionless in the mud. 

Inside it, unseen, unfelt, and silent as prayer, the light was running.
